title: The W Is Playing Deeper — and It's Changing What Can Be Predicted
dek: Rotations are half a player longer this season. Skills stayed stable; roles didn't. That trade shapes everything from box scores to projections.
question: How many players does a team actually use, and what does it break when that moves?
headline: Teams are using 9.89 players a game, up from 9.43 — about half a rotation spot more, every team, every night.
body_template: Watch enough 2026 basketball and you feel it before you can name it: more bodies. The numbers agree. WNBA teams are using {{players_per_game_2026}} players a game this season, up from {{players_per_game_prior}} — roughly half a rotation spot more, every team, every night. That sounds small. It isn't.

Minutes are the currency of basketball analysis. Nearly every projection — points, rebounds, fantasy lines, betting props, our own game model — starts by asking who plays and for how long. And minutes just got materially harder to know. In our two-season reliability testing, a player's minutes carried a season-over-season reliability of .905 in the shallower era. This season the same measure sits at .695. Bench minutes are the wild west: .49, a near coin-flip.

Here's the part that matters: the players didn't get less predictable — the coaches did. The skill signals are as stable as ever. Assist rate and defensive rebounding replicate at .95. Shot volume holds at .93. Free-throw trips at .90. What a player IS barely moves year to year. What a player is ASKED TO DO is what's wobbling, because a deeper rotation redistributes role minutes nightly.

We tested the obvious alternative explanations — an injury wave, expansion churn, general volatility — and the depth effect is what survives: the league simply plays more people. It shows up everywhere downstream. Per-game leaderboards flatten, because stars share more of the clock. Counting stats undersell talent more than usual. And per-minute, context-adjusted impact — the numbers we lead with on every card — become the honest way to compare players, because they don't punish someone for a coach's ten-deep bench.

It reshapes our own work too. This is why our minutes model runs on a short adaptive window instead of trusting last month, and why pre-tip availability — knowing who actually dresses, before the ball goes up — is the most valuable input we can capture. In a nine-and-a-half-player league, the difference between a projection and a guess is the rotation news.

The deeper league is also, quietly, a healthier one: fewer 38-minute nights, more developmental burn for the back of rosters, more variance for viewers. But if you consume numbers — fantasy, betting, arguments with your group chat — recalibrate: trust rates over totals, watch the rotation report, and treat any per-game stat this season as a minutes bet in disguise.

method_footer_template: Reliability = season-over-season correlation of player-level rates across matched samples, two seasons of play-by-play (identity-gated lineups, 97% possession coverage). Players-per-game = average distinct players logging minutes per team-game, {{as_of_date}}. Full method in the Glossary.

blowouts.note: team-games decided by fewer than 15 points, the same blowout cut the score-effects dive uses — no second threshold coined here

expansion.note: 13 franchises played both seasons; the expansion clubs are dropped from both sides

season_shape.note: the prior season truncated to its first 99 game-dates, so a season in progress is not compared against a completed one

reliability.source: docs/reports/MODEL_STATE_OF_RECORD.md -- season-over-season reliability table: `minutes` row (prior 0.905, current 0.695), and the `assists`, `shot attempts` and `free-throw attempts` rows beneath it
reliability.note: Replicated findings from the established record, printed as written -- not recomputed by this dive. See `source` for where each figure came from.

chart.caption: The whole distribution slid right by 0.47 of a player — about half a rotation spot. Bars under 10 team-games are marked thin.

method.definition: distinct players logging more than zero minutes, per team per game, averaged over team-games
method.garbage_time: NOT fenced out of the headline on purpose -- a bench emptied in blowouts is one of the explanations this piece has to survive, so it is measured as a robustness check at the existing 15-point blowout cut rather than assumed away

excluded.how: each count is the SAME query with its predicate inverted -- the exhibition fence is the canonical coalesce(is_exhibition, false) = false, the season fence is season_type = 2, and a box-score row with no minutes is a player who dressed rather than a player who was used
